name: Panicum

project_scope.note: B009 Panicum set; P. coloratum is retained only as an introduced/invasive comparison.

study_strategy.warning: Do not identify these from a generic open panicle alone. Read the base, ligule/collar, leaf texture and panicle architecture together.
overlap_cautions: Open panicles occur in several species; inspect base, collar and mature spikelets together.
Master Plant Pool Panicum obtusum is a legacy concept corresponding to Hopia obtusa; do not add a fifth canonical Panicum card.
P. coloratum retains existing introduced/non-native comparison classification; no new range decision.

look_here_first: When a grass looks like switchgrass, don't stop at the giant open panicle. OPEN ONE MATURE COLLAR: P. virgatum shows a dense triangular WHITE HAIR patch on the upper blade base and a short ciliate membrane, with NO true auricles. Then inspect the very OPEN BRANCHED pyramid of many tiny AWNLESS singly pedicelled spikelets and the rhizomatous perennial crown. In the other installed Panicums: P. hallii is shorter, often BLUE-GLAUCOUS, stiffly tufted with a modest panicle; P. capillare is an ANNUAL with hairs over much of its nodes/sheaths and an immense chaotic haze of panicle branches; P. coloratum is introduced African KLEINGRASS with tufted/knotty crown and a finer panicle. At larger-grass level, Indiangrass S. nutans differs in a prominent notched MEMBRANOUS 'rifle-sight' collar, golden narrower plume and BENT AWNS. Johnsongrass may have an open panicle but has different paired spikelets/rhizomes. Avoid cultivars or ornamental color as an identification standard.
shared_genus_traits: Jointed grass culms with leaf sheaths, collars and ligules.
Branched panicles of small spikelets; mature spikelet and glume/lemma details help resolve look-alikes.
Growth base, collar hairs and inflorescence branching distinguish these four learner species better than flower color.

comparison_cards.title: Switchgrass versus Indiangrass and Johnsongrass — collar, awn, spikelet pairing
comparison_cards.look_here_first: At blade base: Switchgrass WHITE TRIANGULAR hair cluster with short ciliate membrane. Indiangrass prominent upright pointed RIFLE-SIGHT membranous ligule. Johnsongrass normally broader developed smooth membrane with no switchgrass hair triangle. Then check seedhead: switchgrass broad airy panicle, individual AWNLESS small singly pedicelled spikelets; Indiangrass narrower golden awned plume with naked sterile pedicels; Johnsongrass pairs developed pedicelled spikelets with sessile units.

field_matrix.switchgrass: Single ovoid ~3–5 mm AWNLESS unit on pedicel
field_matrix.indiangrass: AWNED fertile sessile spikelet + naked sterile pedicel
field_matrix.johnsongrass: Sessile fertile plus developed pedicelled spikelet

visual_comparison.memory_rule: Switchgrass: underground SCALY RHIZOME + triangular white blade-base HAIR patch + huge open head and real single AWNLESS spikelets with a lower staminate/sterile floret and upper bisexual fertile floret. crew_key: Open a mature collar: switchgrass has the triangular blade-base hair patch; do not mistake it for true auricles.
Check growth base: switchgrass forms rhizomatous stands; witchgrass is annual; Hall's panicgrass forms stiff glaucous perennial bunches; kleingrass has a knotty perennial crown.

Compare mature panicles: witchgrass extremely diffuse and lax, Hall's stiffer ascending branches, switchgrass broad open pyramidal, kleingrass finer open panicle; these overlap, so never key from panicle alone.
For doubtful plants, photograph ligule/collar with mm scale, entire basal crown, panicle branch junction and mature spikelets before assigning species.
specific_photo_gaps: Switchgrass rhizome/base and precise membranous ligule contour remain underdocumented.
Matched scaled collars and mature spikelet macros for P. hallii versus P. coloratum are needed.
Confirm diagnostic photo arrow placements against actual image pixels; no new arrows assumed.
scientific_guardrails: P. coloratum remains introduced comparison; no native status change.
Legacy Panicum obtusum routes to Hopia obtusa; do not duplicate.
No species identity is inferred from general habitat or panicle silhouette alone.
